newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-UK's PowerGen targets Indian investments.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-UK's PowerGen targets Indian investments.

text.p: UK-based private generating firm PowerGen Plc is likely to quadruple its investments in the Indian power sector in the next three to four years, a senior company official said on Wednesday.

"We have around $50-60 million invested in India in Gujarat and we expect to quadruple that amount in the next three or four years," Peter Hughes, managing director of PowerGen's overseas business, told Reuters in an interview.
"We think and hope we can invest in 3,000 to 4,000 MWs of power in India," he said.
The 655 MW Gujarat Torrent Energy Corporation project in western India is a venture of the Torrent Group, PowerGen, Siemens AG and Gujarat Power Corporation Ltd. The UK firm holds 20 percent.
"The project is going very well. It should start commissioning in October-November," Hughes said.
He said PowerGen was bidding for two more projects in Gujarat -- a 700 MW gas project and a 1,000 MW coal project to be commissioned in two stages of 500 MW.
"We are also looking at projects in a number of states. We believe India has got great potential. Things are starting to move forward," Hughes said.
But Hughes said frequent bureaucratic delays were a major hinderance to foreign investments in the power sector.
"It's the bureaucracy. It's just getting people to take decisions. We recognised that when we arrived. You need a conscious political will to change these things," he said.
PowerGen's projects in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh state in central India have been delayed.
Hughes said PowerGen's project in Uttar Pradesh -- a joint venture with the leading Aditya Birla group -- was unlikely to take off soon.
"The project is still a current project but I wouldn't describe it as a live project," he said.
Insitutional lenders to the project have demanded a corporate guarantee due to the poor financial status of the state electricity board. Both both partners have refused to provide this guarantee.
A guarantee would force the two firms to meet all financial commitments to the lenders if the electricity board defaulted.
Hughes said several solutions had been suggested.

"The government could actually put in place an escrow arrangement which has been suggested," he said. Another remedy would be to ask some of the larger consumers to provide credit support for the project, he said.
"There's a lot of discussion going on. The venture is on the backburner."
He said the Madhya Pradesh was being held up by constraints fixing commercial agreements to supply coal for the project.
"It's a matter of how quickly things are done," Hughes said.
The state-run Coal India, which has a monopoly to supply these services, gives no guarantee of regular supplies.
"The various ministries have been asking Coal India to put commercial frameworks in place but its taking a rather long time," he said.
"But we are patient people," he added.
